notes: Stopped: the four parallel simulations ran in lockstep, and a step that skipped through a quiet spell made the others wait, so it ran at about 16 decisions a second (17 hours for a million). Skipping is now capped per step; replaced by stage1a-02. Its head start agreed with the speed-only controller 89% of the time.

Tested at 100k decisions on 40 unseen sessions against the speed-only rules controller: 83 separation losses against 81, 64 gaps inside the minimum against 41, 0 speed instructions. Its best choice was always 'leave the speed alone': the head start copied a controller that leaves speeds alone about 9 times in 10. No speed control did almost as well on separation, so most losses come from the planner releasing aircraft only about 4 NM apart. Replaced by stage1a-03: speeds chosen as targets, a weighted head start, and more room from the planner.

Target speeds (160-250 kt in 10 kt values, inside the band) instead of steps; head start weighted towards speed changes; planner slots about 4.5 NM apart with fixed paths. The machine was restarted at about 19:00, 181k decisions in; resumed from the 100k copy (the 81k decisions in between are set aside), so 4.6 hours includes about 0.4 hours lost. Tested on 40 unseen sessions against the speed-only rules controller (56 separation losses, gap error 2.44 NM, 3.9 instructions per arrival): head start 46 / 2.36 / 3.6, 100k 52 / 2.41 / 3.7, 300k 97 / 2.68 / 3.9, 500k 53 / 2.51 / 4.1, 750k 53 / 2.44 / 4.3, final 52 / 2.36 / 4.7. Gate not passed; up to about 20 losses either way is within the noise of 40 sessions. Practice made it more random (chance of its top choice 95% after the head start, 57% at the end) and no better.

Holding stacks like real ones (first come first served, lowest leaves first, levels only once vacated, climb out of a taken level); only aircraft whose speed the AI gives count in its action probabilities and uncertainty; uncertainty reward 0.001; fading penalty (0.5 to 0.05) for moving away from the head start. Tested on 120 unseen sessions against the speed-only rules controller (179 separation losses, 40 at the stacks; gap error 2.42 NM; 91 gaps inside the minimum): head start 168 / 2.38 / 74, 100k 181 / 2.39 / 81, 300k 176 / 2.40 / 74, 500k 189 / 2.36 / 81, 750k 172 / 2.40 / 80, final 167 / 2.40 / 80. No difference beyond chance (95% range about +/-30 losses); gate not passed. Stable this time (no drift to random choices) but no better than its head start. Leaving every speed alone on the same sessions: 218 losses, 222 gaps inside the minimum, 25 wake infringements, 139 go-arounds: speed control matters for the gaps, but most losses happen whatever the speeds.

Stage 1b: the AI turns aircraft onto base (plus speeds) in a world timed with the wind that releases aircraft from the hold eagerly; competitor: the eager speed-then-stretch rule. Same learning as stage1a-04 (only effective choices count, fading pull to the head start). Restarted at the head start: with the rule's turns counting 10 times it agreed with only 83% of the rule's waits (turning early); now counted once. Stopped: its head start flew much worse than the eager rule it copied (120 test sessions: 217 separation losses against 150, 126 go-arounds against 64, gap error 3.06 NM against 2.47), so it had not learned when the rule turns base, and practice pulled it back towards that copy. Replaced by stage1b-02, whose AI also sees how far each aircraft is from the rule's planned base turn.

Stage 1b, second run: as stage1b-01, but the AI also sees the planner's base turn (distance to it, and whether it would turn before the next decision), and its head start weights every turn-or-wait choice 10 times. Head start on 120 test sessions: 180 separation losses against the eager rule's 150 (within chance), 98 go-arounds against 64. After practice it fell further behind: 100k 201 losses / 101 go-arounds, 300k 204 / 106. Why: a third of its base turns (105 of 320 on 20 sessions) were made for it at the RMA edge; once it missed the planner's point it never turned, because copying the rule showed it no aircraft past that point, and those aircraft then joined final late and close (go-arounds for being too close to the aircraft ahead: 17 against the rule's 6). Replaced by stage1b-03, in which the planner's turn is the default and the AI chooses as planned, turn now or not yet.

Stage 1b, third run: the planner's base turn is the default; for each aircraft on the downwind the AI chooses as planned, turn now or not yet (taking the turn over). Head start copies 'as planned' with 2% of the target on the other two. Otherwise as stage1b-02. The machine was restarted twice (about 02:00 and 06:37); it carried on from its working copies at 150k and 900k (42k decisions of episodes set aside). Tested on 120 unseen sessions against the eager rule (150 separation losses, 64 go-arounds, 1,739 landed): head start 141 / 72 / 1,742, 100k 146 / 74 / 1,737, 500k 141 / 71 / 1,735, 750k 157 / 74 / 1,735, final 145 / 68 / 1,737. Level with the rule throughout, no difference beyond chance; gate not passed. In practice it chose 'turn now' about 0.1 times per arrival and 'not yet' almost never (it only acts in the 10 s before the planner would turn an aircraft).

Stage 2's first run: the AI adjusts the planner's headings (5/10 deg), levels (1,000 ft) and speeds (10/20 kt); measured pilots, model look-ahead; head start copies as planned with 3% smoothing; stopped at 450k: its choices never moved from as planned (still about 97% everywhere), so its tests matched the competitor exactly
